enonce_markdown: Given $\mathbf a=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$, find the scalar product $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3$. The result is a number (a scalar), not a vector.

### Solution

$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=(2)(1)+(-1)(4)+(3)(-2)=2-4-6=-8$.

The option $2\mathbf i-4\mathbf j-6\mathbf k$ multiplies components but does not add them; $4$ comes from a sign slip on the last term, and $8$ from dropping the sign.

enonce_markdown: Find the angle between the vectors $\mathbf u=\mathbf i+\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf v=\mathbf j+\mathbf k$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|}$, then take $\theta=\cos^{-1}$ of the result.

### Solution

$\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=(1)(0)+(1)(1)+(0)(1)=1$, $|\mathbf u|=\sqrt2$, $|\mathbf v|=\sqrt2$.
$$\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt2\sqrt2}=\frac12\Rightarrow\theta=60^\circ.$$
Since the scalar product is positive the angle is acute, which rules out $120^\circ$.

enonce_markdown: Given $\mathbf a=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$, find $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Expand the determinant with rows $\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k$; $\mathbf a$; $\mathbf b$, remembering that the $\mathbf j$ term carries a minus sign. Check that the result is perpendicular to both vectors.

### Solution

$$\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&-1&3\\1&4&-2\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf i[(-1)(-2)-(3)(4)]-\mathbf j[(2)(-2)-(3)(1)]+\mathbf k[(2)(4)-(-1)(1)]$$
$$=-10\mathbf i+7\mathbf j+9\mathbf k.$$
Check: $(-10,7,9)\cdot(2,-1,3)=-20-7+27=0$ and $(-10,7,9)\cdot(1,4,-2)=-10+28-18=0$.

A wrong sign on the $\mathbf j$ term gives $(-10,-7,9)$; computing $\mathbf b\times\mathbf a$ gives $(10,-7,-9)$; adding instead of subtracting $(-1)(1)$ in the $\mathbf k$ term gives $7$.

enonce_markdown: The points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,1,1)$ and $C(2,3,0)$ are the vertices of a triangle. Use a vector product to find the exact area of triangle $ABC$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The area of a triangle with sides $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is $\tfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$.

### Solution

$\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,1,-1)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(1,3,-2)$.
$$\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&1&-1\\1&3&-2\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf i(-2+3)-\mathbf j(-4+1)+\mathbf k(6-1)=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+5\mathbf k.$$
Its modulus is $\sqrt{1+9+25}=\sqrt{35}$, so
$$\boxed{\text{Area}=\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}\approx2.96\text{ square units}}.$$

enonce_markdown: The vectors $\mathbf a=2\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+6\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=-4\mathbf i+p\mathbf j+q\mathbf k$ are parallel. Find $p+q$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Two non-zero vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other, equivalently $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\mathbf 0$. Find the multiplier from a component that is known in both vectors.

### Solution

Let $\mathbf b=\lambda\mathbf a$. The $\mathbf i$ components give $-4=2\lambda$, so $\lambda=-2$.

Then $p=-3\lambda=6$ and $q=6\lambda=-12$, so $p+q=-6$.

Check: $\mathbf b=(-4,6,-12)=-2(2,-3,6)$. A sign slip on $\lambda$ ($\lambda=2$) gives $p=-6$, $q=12$ and $p+q=6$; adding magnitudes gives $\pm18$.

enonce_markdown: Find the perpendicular distance from the point $P(3,3,2)$ to the line through $A(1,0,1)$ with direction vector $\mathbf d=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

If $\theta$ is the angle between $\overrightarrow{AP}$ and $\mathbf d$, the distance is $|\overrightarrow{AP}|\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\mathbf d|}{|\mathbf d|}$.

### Solution

$\overrightarrow{AP}=(2,3,1)$, and
$$\overrightarrow{AP}\times\mathbf d=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&3&1\\2&1&2\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf i(6-1)-\mathbf j(4-2)+\mathbf k(2-6)=5\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-4\mathbf k.$$
Its modulus is $\sqrt{25+4+16}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5$ and $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3$.
$$\boxed{\text{distance}=\frac{3\sqrt5}{3}=\sqrt5\approx2.24}$$
Check: the foot of the perpendicular is at $t=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|^2}=\dfrac{4+3+2}{9}=1$, i.e. $(3,1,3)$, and the distance from it to $P$ is $\sqrt{0+4+1}=\sqrt5$.
